blocks.text: What bleed and slug mean for a print PDF

Bleed is extra artwork that runs past the trim line. The printer cuts the paper down to the trim size. If your art stops at the trim, a small shift in the cut shows a white sliver on the edge. Bleed gives the cutter room to be slightly off. Slug is the strip outside the trim and bleed. It holds job information that gets cut off the finished piece, like the job name or a date.

A common spec is 0.125 in of bleed on all four sides. The University of Minnesota print center recommends that value in its setup guide. The guide says to add 0.25 in to both the width and the height of the trim size. A 5 x 7 in card needs a 5.25 x 7.25 in file. Your printer may ask for something else, so read their spec before you start.
Set bleed in InDesign with Document Setup

Start in InDesign, not at export. Bleed is a document setting, so set it before you place artwork. Open File > Document Setup, or press ⌥⌘P. Find the Bleed and Slug section. Enter 0.125 in in each bleed field. Keep all four values the same unless your printer asks for something else.

items: Open File > Document Setup, or press ⌥⌘P.
Select the Bleed and Slug section in the dialog.
Type 0.125 in in Top, Bottom, Inside and Outside. If Facing Pages is off, the fields read Left and Right.
Click OK. InDesign draws a red bleed guide around each page.

blocks.text: The red guide does not stretch anything. It only shows where the bleed starts. Your art still has to reach it. Many designers stop after this step and assume the bleed exists in the file. It does not, until the artwork covers that area.
Extend artwork past the trim to the bleed guide

Any element that touches the page edge must continue past the trim. That includes background colors, gradients, photos, and thin rules. Select the frame and move or resize it so it runs past the page edge to the red guide. A photo should cover the whole frame, bleed included. Zoom in on each corner before you move on.
Text works the other way. Keep headlines and body copy well inside the trim. Anything near the edge can be cut in finishing. Ask your printer for their safe margin, and keep text inside it.
Export a print PDF with bleed and marks

The export is where bleed often gets lost. InDesign has its own bleed choice in the PDF export dialog. If that box is not ticked, your PDF can leave without the bleed you set in Document Setup. Menu names can shift between versions, so compare these steps with your screen.

items: In Preset, choose Highest Quality Print. Your version may use a slightly different name.
Click Marks and Bleed in the left column.
Tick Use Document Bleed Settings. Check that each value reads 0.125 in.
Decide on crop marks with your printer. Some want them, and some do not.
Click Export, then open the file and check it.

blocks.title: Check the page size
blocks.text: If the exported page is the same size as the trim, the bleed did not come along. Re-export with Use Document Bleed Settings ticked, then check the size again.

Open the PDF in Acrobat or Preview and look at the page size and the edges. A file with bleed is larger than the trim. Use the file name to track the version, so you do not send an old export by mistake.
Slug settings and what goes in the slug

The slug is the area outside the trim and bleed. In InDesign, the same Bleed and Slug section of Document Setup holds slug values. The UMN guide mentions this dialog for slug but gives no slug values, so use the numbers from your printer. Put job information there, not inside the trim.

Common slug content includes the job name, the date, the page count, and a color bar if your printer asks for one. Slug content is cut away in finishing. Do not put anything there that you need to keep.

When you export, you may see an Include Slug Area option in the Marks and Bleed tab. That option name came from search results, so check it in your version. If the printer does not ask for slug material, leave the option off.
Worked example: a 5 x 7 in card

Say the finished card is 5 x 7 in. In InDesign, keep the page at 5 x 7 in. Set bleed to 0.125 in on each side. InDesign draws the bleed outside the page. When you tick Use Document Bleed Settings on export, the bleed comes along with the PDF. Your art must reach the bleed guide on every edge, so the cutter has room.

blocks.caption: Add 0.25 in to width and height for a 0.125 in bleed. Rule from the UMN print center.

blocks.text: The added 0.25 in matters when the bleed lives in the canvas, which is how Photoshop works. In InDesign the page stays at trim size, so you do not add 0.25 in to the page itself.
Illustrator and Photoshop bleed settings

In Illustrator, set bleed to 0.125 in in Document Setup. Then choose File > Save As, pick Adobe PDF as the format, and tick Use Document Bleed Settings in the export options. The UMN guide gives these steps. Check the bleed values again in the PDF dialog before you save.

In Photoshop, you build the bleed into the canvas. Open Image > Canvas Size, or press ⌥⌘C. For a 5 x 7 in card, set the width to 5.25 in and the height to 7.25 in, as the UMN guide describes. Set 300 ppi on new documents. Then fill the new edges, because the added strip may come in empty. More on Photoshop workflows is in the [Photoshop for designers](/for/designers/photoshop) guide.
Check the PDF before it goes to the printer

Preflight catches some problems, but it cannot prove that your art reaches the bleed. Adobe Community members said Acrobat Preflight and similar tools do not check bleed coverage reliably. One member called a preflight profile far from foolproof for this job. Run preflight for fonts, images, and color, then check the edges yourself.

For the visual check, open the PDF at a large zoom. Look at each corner and each edge. Confirm that backgrounds and photos reach the page edge. Then confirm that text sits inside the trim. If your Acrobat version offers a page boxes view, use it to compare the boxes. Menu names vary, so check Adobe's current help.
Mistakes that cause bleed and slug problems

items: Setting bleed in Document Setup, then forgetting the export box.
Placing a photo that stops at the trim, so the bleed shows white.
Using the trim size as the canvas size in Photoshop or Illustrator.
Leaving text too close to the edge, where finishing can cut it.
Putting working notes in the slug, then sending the file with the notes still in it.
Reusing an old template after the printer changed its spec.
Sending the file without checking the exported page size.

blocks.text: Most of these show up only on the finished piece. The document window shows your art, not the cut. That is why checking the exported PDF matters more than checking the layout on screen.
What bleed errors cost and what the numbers show

Nobody has measured how often designers hit bleed or slug errors, or what those errors cost. The numbers that exist come from vendors and informal polls. Dalim, a preflight vendor, says manual preflight takes several minutes per file, compared with seconds for automated checks. Dalim cites no study for that claim.

A 2011 poll on the Prepressure website asked 127 voters whether customer files were print-ready. 57% said no, and most of the time the files needed adjustment. The poll is informal and self-selected, and it is about 15 years old. Treat it as a warning, not a rate.

Dalim also says a reprint can take days. Its example is about blurry images, not bleed. A bleed error can still force a reprint if the cut shows white edges on a color block. Ask your printer how long a reprint takes before you send a rush job.
Edge cases for bleed and slug in print PDF

A full-bleed photo needs to cover the bleed on every side. A photo with a small margin looks fine on screen and fails at the cut. Crop the photo so the subject stays inside the trim, then let the image run into the bleed.

Thin rules and borders need care. A rule that sits right on the trim line can end up partly cut. Move rules inside the trim, or extend them into the bleed. Ask whether the printer wants a border at all.
If your printer gives a spec in millimeters, use their number. Then check the page size after you convert. The UMN guide uses inches, so keep one unit through the whole file to avoid mistakes.

If you work in Affinity Publisher, the guidance online conflicts. One guide says to set bleed in Document Setup and re-tick it on export. Another says to skip printer marks for some online printers. Follow your printer's spec, and test one file before the full run.
Get the bleed spec from your printer first

The 0.125 in value is a common default, not a rule for every printer. Email the shop or read the product page for the spec. Ask three questions: how much bleed, whether they want crop marks, and whether they want slug material. Save the answers with the job files, so the next designer does not have to guess.
Build a bleed-ready template

Once you have the spec, save it as a template. Set the page size to the trim, set bleed and slug in Document Setup, then save the file as an InDesign template (.indt). Next time, start from the template. The bleed value is already set, so you skip the step that gets missed.
Where Lazur fits in the bleed workflow

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on your screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can point at the control you need. Ask how to do a step, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. It does not click buttons or change the file for you.

That fits the parts of this job people forget. Ask Lazur to show you the bleed fields in Document Setup, or to walk through the export tab. Hold fn to dictate notes for the printer without typing them. The file, the values, and the decisions stay with you, which is how it should be on a print job.
What to do next

Pick one job this week. Get the printer's spec, set bleed in your document, export one test PDF, and check every edge at high zoom. Then save the setup as a template. faq.question: How much bleed does InDesign need for a print PDF?
faq.answer: The University of Minnesota print center recommends 0.125 in on all four sides. Set that in Document Setup, then ask your printer to confirm, because shops can publish their own spec.

faq.question: Do I need a slug for every print job?
faq.answer: No. Use slug only when the printer asks for job information or color bars. Set the values in the Bleed and Slug section, and turn on the slug option at export only if the printer wants it.

faq.question: Why does my exported PDF have no bleed?
faq.answer: A likely reason is that Use Document Bleed Settings is off in the Marks and Bleed tab. Setting bleed in Document Setup alone does not change the export. Re-export with the box ticked and check the page size.

faq.question: Can Acrobat Preflight check bleed for me?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Adobe Community members said preflight profiles cannot tell whether artwork reaches the bleed. Use preflight for fonts and images, then inspect each edge yourself at high zoom.

faq.question: Does Lazur change my InDesign file?
faq.answer: No. Lazur sees your screen when you hold ⌥⌘, points at controls, and guides you one click at a time. You click, you type, and you decide the settings.

costs.title: Time spent on each file
costs.text: Dalim, a preflight vendor, says manual preflight takes several minutes per file, compared with seconds for automated checks. The company cites no study. Treat it as a rough sense of effort, not a measured cost.

costs.title: Reprints and late jobs
costs.text: Dalim says a reprint can take days, but its example is about blurry images, not bleed. A bleed error can force a reprint too, if the cut shows white edges. Ask your printer how long a reprint takes before you send a rush job.

costs.title: Cut-off text and white edges
costs.text: A headline cut by the trim, or a white edge on a color block, is easy for a client to see. No public source measures how often this happens, so your own record is the best guide you have.

costs.title: Client trust
costs.text: A print run that comes back with edge problems can cost you the next job. There is no public number for this. It shows up in whether the client asks for proofs next time, and in how much they trust your files.

costs.title: How often this happens
costs.text: No survey measures how often designers hit bleed or slug errors. A 2011 poll on one prepress site found 57% of 127 voters said customer files usually needed adjustment. It is informal and about 15 years old, so use it as a warning, not a rate.

causes.title: Bleed set in the wrong place
causes.text: Bleed in Document Setup does not change artwork. It only draws the guide. Designers who set the value and then forget to extend their art end up with a red line that nothing reaches. The same problem happens in Photoshop when the canvas is trimmed rather than enlarged.

causes.title: The export box is unticked
causes.text: The PDF export dialog has its own bleed choice. If Use Document Bleed Settings is not ticked in Marks and Bleed, the PDF can go out without the bleed you set earlier. The file still looks normal in the layout window, so the gap is easy to miss.

causes.title: Artwork stops at the trim by habit
causes.text: Many layouts are built to the trim line because that is the size on the brief. Backgrounds, photos, and color blocks get drawn to the page edge, not past it. Under time pressure, the bleed gets missed.

causes.title: Placed files are too short
causes.text: A photo placed in a frame can cover the frame but still stop before the bleed. A placed logo or PDF can do the same. Check placed files at the bleed line, not only at the trim.

causes.title: Printer specs differ or change
causes.text: One shop asks for 0.125 in, another asks for a different number, and an old template keeps the old value. Designers who reuse templates often copy the bleed setting without checking the current spec.

causes.title: Preflight gives false comfort
causes.text: A preflight profile can pass a file that has no bleed coverage. Adobe Community members said the tools cannot reliably check bleed. A passing check does not prove that your art reaches the edge.

causes.title: Slug and bleed get mixed up
causes.text: Some designers put job notes in the slug and forget that slug is cut away. Others pull slug content into the trim. Both mix-ups make the file harder to check, and both show up at the printer rather than on the screen.

fixes.title: Set bleed in Document Setup first
fixes.text: Open File > Document Setup, or press ⌥⌘P. Enter 0.125 in in each bleed field unless the printer asks for another value. Set this before you place artwork, so the red guide is there when you extend your files to it.

fixes.title: Extend every edge to the bleed guide
fixes.text: Select each background, photo, and color block that touches the page edge. Resize or move it so it runs past the edge to the red guide. Zoom in on each corner. A shape that stops at the trim is the most common visible failure.

fixes.title: Tick Use Document Bleed Settings on export
fixes.text: Choose File > Export, pick Adobe PDF (Print), and open Marks and Bleed. Tick Use Document Bleed Settings and confirm 0.125 in on each side. Without that box, the PDF can miss the bleed you set in the document.

fixes.title: Build bleed into the canvas in Photoshop
fixes.text: Use Image > Canvas Size, or press ⌥⌘C. For a 0.125 in bleed on each side, add 0.25 in to the width and to the height. Set 300 ppi on new documents, then fill the new edges with image or background color.

fixes.title: Inspect the exported PDF at high zoom
fixes.text: Open the exported file, not the layout. Check each corner and each edge for white slivers and cut text. Confirm that the page is larger than the trim when bleed is included. Export again if anything is off, then check the new file the same way.

fixes.title: Keep a template with the spec built in
fixes.text: Save a template with bleed, slug, and page size already set to the printer's spec. Name it with the printer's name and the date you checked the spec. Starting from a template removes the setup step that is easiest to forget.

fixes.title: Ask for a proof on larger jobs
fixes.text: On a bigger run, ask the printer whether they will check the file and send a proof before the full print. A proof shows cut problems that a screen does not show. Compare it with the trim size you designed to.

plan.title: Get the printer spec
plan.text: Email the printer or open their product page. Ask for the bleed size, crop mark rules, and slug needs. Save the answers in the job folder, so the spec is in writing before you start the layout.

plan.title: Set up the document
plan.text: Open File > Document Setup, enter the bleed value on all four sides, and extend backgrounds and photos to the red guide. Keep text well inside the trim. Save the file as a template for the next job.
